Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- The former Utah state trooper suspected in a series of roadway shootings earlier this week died Wednesday, the Dallas County Medical Examiner's Office said. CNN affiliate KSL in Salt Lake City, Utah, provided this file photo of the Dallas suspect, Brian Smith. Police said Tuesday that Brian Smith attempted suicide after Monday's shootings. Smith was brought to a local hospital in serious condition, officials said . At 7 p.m. Wednesday Smith died at Parkland Hospital, the medical examiner's office said. An autopsy is slated for Thursday. Two people were killed in the shootings along a three-mile stretch on and near the LBJ Freeway, about 10 miles northeast of downtown Dallas. Police used ballistic tests to link Smith, a 12-year veteran of the Utah state police, to three of the four shootings, Dallas Police Lt. Craig Miller said Tuesday. Miller said Smith was a suspect in both nonfatal shootings and one of the fatal shootings. He said it was unclear if Smith was a suspect in the fatal shooting that occurred first. The first attack occurred in the city of Garland at about 5:41 p.m. Victim Jorge Lopez, 20, was sitting in his Nissan at a traffic light in Garland when a man in a pickup pulled alongside him and fired shots into his car, killing him, Officer Joe Harn of the Garland police said. A few minutes later and two miles away on the LBJ Freeway, a gunman fired at two tractor-trailers. While one driver escaped injuries, William Scott Miller, 42, of Frankfort, Kentucky, was shot to death behind the wheel of a United Van Lines truck, police said. "He was going to be traveling home," Lt. Miller said. "He was about to park his rig. He was going to get on a plane to fly to be with his wife and children for the Christmas season and then come back to this location." Miller called the truck driver a hero because he was able to control his rig before he died -- preventing other motorists from being hurt. The fourth attack came a mile west on LBJ Freeway, where gunfire shattered the windshield of another tractor-trailer. The bullets missed the driver, but flying glass caused minor cuts, police said. Smith, 37, left his trooper job in Utah after he was caught abusing alcohol and drugs, CNN affiliate WFAA reported, citing an official report. The sergeant began using drugs and alcohol after his patrol car was rear-ended while he was writing a ticket, according to the report by Utah Peace Officers Standards and Training. He moved to Texas shortly afterward, the station said. Harn told WFAA that Smith's wife had phoned police Monday to say her husband was suicidal and driving around with a gun. Police were able to locate him using cell phone transmission towers. A three-hour stand-off followed, ending when Smith shot himself in the head, Harn said.

CNN affiliate KSL in Salt Lake City, Utah, supplied a file image of the Dallas suspect, Brian Smith. Authorities said Tuesday that Smith tried to take his own life after the shootings on Monday. Officials said he was transported to a nearby hospital in serious condition.

The medical examiner’s office said Smith died at Parkland Hospital at 7 p.m. Wednesday. An autopsy was scheduled for Thursday.

The shootings left two people dead along a roughly three-mile area on and near the LBJ Freeway, about 10 miles northeast of downtown Dallas.

Miller said Smith was considered a suspect in both shootings in which the victims survived, as well as in one of the fatal attacks. He added that investigators had not determined whether Smith was connected to the first fatal shooting.

That initial attack happened in Garland at about 5:41 p.m. Officer Joe Harn of the Garland Police Department said 20-year-old Jorge Lopez was stopped at a traffic light in his Nissan when a man in a pickup truck pulled up beside him and fired into the vehicle, killing him.

Minutes later, about two miles away on the LBJ Freeway, someone opened fire on two tractor-trailers. One driver was not injured, but police said 42-year-old William Scott Miller of Frankfort, Kentucky, was fatally shot while driving a United Van Lines truck.

“He was going to be traveling home,” Lt. Miller said. “He was about to park his rig. He was going to get on a plane to fly to be with his wife and children for the Christmas season and then come back to this location.”

Miller described the truck driver as a hero, saying he managed to keep control of the rig before he died, which kept other drivers from being harmed.

The fourth shooting occurred about a mile farther west on the LBJ Freeway, where shots broke the windshield of another tractor-trailer. Police said the bullets did not hit the driver, though shattered glass caused minor cuts.

Smith, 37, had left his job as a trooper in Utah after being found to have abused alcohol and drugs, CNN affiliate WFAA reported, referencing an official report. According to a report from Utah Peace Officers Standards and Training, the sergeant began using drugs and alcohol after his patrol car was struck from behind while he was writing a ticket. WFAA said he relocated to Texas not long after that.

Harn told WFAA that Smith’s wife called police Monday to report that her husband was suicidal and was driving around while armed. Officers tracked him through cell phone transmission towers.

A standoff lasting three hours followed, Harn said, and it ended when Smith shot himself in the head.

**By CNN-style news staff**  
**Dallas, Texas** — A former Utah state trooper has been linked through ballistics evidence to multiple roadway shootings in the Dallas area, according to law enforcement officials, raising questions about whether a series of seemingly random attacks on drivers may have been connected.

Brian Smith, who previously worked as a trooper in Utah, came under scrutiny after investigators examined shell casings and bullet fragments recovered from several shooting scenes near Dallas. Ballistics testing matched evidence from multiple incidents to the same firearm or firearms associated with Smith, authorities said.

The shootings occurred on or near major roadways, where drivers reported being fired upon while traveling through the Dallas area. In some cases, vehicles were struck by bullets; in others, investigators recovered evidence from the roadside or from damaged cars. Officials have not publicly detailed a motive, and it remains unclear whether the victims were targeted or chosen at random.

Investigators say the ballistics link became a key break in the case. Forensic firearms analysis can compare markings left on bullets and cartridge casings when a gun is fired. Those microscopic markings can help authorities determine whether rounds from different crime scenes were fired from the same weapon.

Smith’s background in law enforcement added a troubling dimension to the investigation. As a former trooper, he would have had training and experience with firearms, traffic enforcement and roadway procedures. Authorities have not said whether his prior law enforcement service played any role in the shootings or in how the incidents unfolded.

The case has drawn attention because roadway shootings can be especially difficult to investigate. Crime scenes may span miles of highway, victims may not immediately realize they have been shot at, and evidence can be scattered or lost in traffic. Investigators often rely on surveillance footage, witness reports, license plate readers, shell casings and ballistic testing to build connections between incidents.

Law enforcement agencies in the Dallas area worked together to compare reports of similar shootings, review forensic evidence and determine whether the incidents were part of a broader pattern. The ballistics findings, officials said, helped tie the cases together and connect them to Smith.

Authorities have not released full details about the number of shootings linked to the investigation, the timeline of the attacks or whether additional suspects are being sought. Court records and police statements are expected to provide more information as the case proceeds.

Smith has not been convicted in connection with the shootings. Like all defendants, he is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in court.

The investigation remains ongoing.
